items.x_text:
Symantec trapped an AI attack agent that hijacks exposed OpenAI-style model endpoints as its planning brain. Built for up to 100,000 unattended steps, 74 offensive tools. The endpoint owner pays for the inference.

#AISecurity #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Your exposed AI model could be planning someone else's attack. And you'd pay the bill. 🤖

Symantec's Threat Hunter Team caught an attack agent in an AI honeypot:
→ It scans for endpoints that accept OpenAI-style requests with no authentication, or with a stolen key
→ The victim's model becomes the "reasoning engine that plans and drives the attack"
→ Built to run up to 100,000 steps unattended, with 74 offensive tool definitions
→ The operators called its scan-infect-mine loop "Skynet mode"
→ Symantec has no evidence of real-world use yet, and hasn't attributed it

What to do: put authentication on every model endpoint, rotate any API key that's ever been exposed, and alert on inference usage you can't explain.

cover.hook: Researcher: one hacked device could reach root on other Tailscale servers.
cover.sub: Erica Windisch's "Tailworm" report, tested in a lab. No patch and no CVE yet. Tailscale says it is working on fixes.

slides.title: What was reported
slides.body: Cyberdione Labs' Erica Windisch tested Tailscale 1.104.2 and headscale 0.29.5 in a lab. With Tailscale SSH port forwarding on, an allowed device could reach root-only sockets and run commands as root.

slides.title: The conditions
slides.body: It needs Tailscale SSH with port forwarding enabled, plus an attacker-controlled device that your ACLs let reach the target. Capturing an enrollment key fully worked only on networks without Tailnet Lock.

slides.label: findings in the Tailworm report
slides.note: Not independently reproduced; some researchers dispute the "wormable" claim

slides.title: What Tailscale says
slides.body: VP of Engineering Mike Shaver said Tailscale has found issues it is working to fix, and is "not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH." No bulletin or fixed version yet.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Turn off SSH port forwarding where you can
Swap broad tag-based SSH grants for single source-to-destination rules
Enable Tailnet Lock and node-key expiry
On headscale 0.29.5, treat every SSH grant as root

items.question: Do you know which of your devices can SSH into which servers?
items.x_text:
Tailscale SSH: a researcher's "Tailworm" report says one compromised device could reach root on other servers via port forwarding. Lab-tested, no patch or CVE yet; Tailscale says it's working on fixes.

#VulnerabilityManagement #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
One hacked device. Root on your other servers. That's the claim. 🔓

A "Tailworm" report from Erica Windisch (Cyberdione Labs) targets Tailscale SSH:
→ Lab tests on Tailscale 1.104.2 and headscale 0.29.5
→ With SSH port forwarding on, an allowed device could reach root-only sockets and run root commands
→ Grabbing an enrollment key fully worked only without Tailnet Lock
→ No patch, no CVE, not independently reproduced yet
→ Tailscale says it found issues it's fixing, but isn't telling everyone to disable Tailscale SSH

#AISecurity #DataBreach
items.ig_caption:
3,182 patients. One spreadsheet. One unapproved AI tool. 🏥

Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center is notifying patients:
→ A worker uploaded a spreadsheet of patient information to a public AI platform the hospital hadn't approved
→ It covered patients treated May to September 2026: names, admission dates, medications, record and account numbers, providers
→ No Social Security numbers or financial account details, the hospital says
→ Found the same day (21 Sept); the data was deleted from the tool and the AI company asked to delete it
→ Letters went out 22 Oct with 12 months of credit monitoring

What to do: give staff an approved AI tool, block uploads to unapproved ones, and train people on what never goes in a prompt.

cover.hook: DreamHost reset email and FTP passwords. File Manager is still offline.
cover.sub: An incident open since 23 Oct hit File Manager, webmail and FTP/SFTP. DreamHost hasn't said what caused it.

slides.title: What happened
slides.body: On 23 Oct DreamHost began investigating connectivity issues in its File Manager. It widened to webmail sign-outs and FTP/SFTP access, and some email and FTP/SFTP passwords were reset as a precaution.

slides.title: Where it stands
slides.body: By 24 Oct resets for affected email and FTP/SFTP users were complete. On 25 Oct most instruction emails had gone out. The File Manager was still unavailable, with no restoration time given.

slides.label: incident opened. File Manager still down on 25 Oct

slides.title: Watch for fake resets
slides.body: DreamHost says it will never email you asking for your password or ask you to log in through a link. Ignore reset emails you didn't request and set new passwords in the panel yourself.

slides.title: Do this today
items: Set new email and SFTP passwords at panel.dreamhost.com
Ignore password-reset emails you didn't ask for
Review recent FTP logins and file changes on your sites
Never reuse your hosting password anywhere else

items.ig_caption:

From DreamHost's status page:
→ 23 Oct: investigating connectivity issues in the File Manager, then webmail sign-outs and FTP/SFTP access
→ Some email and FTP/SFTP passwords were reset as a precaution
→ 24 Oct: resets for affected users complete; owners set new passwords in the panel
→ 25 Oct: File Manager still unavailable, no restoration time; no cause given yet

What to do: set new passwords at panel.dreamhost.com yourself, ignore reset emails you didn't request (DreamHost says it never asks for your password by email), and check recent FTP logins.

items.ig_caption:
Your Plex server could be mining crypto for someone else. ⛏️

CISA warns attackers are actively exploiting Plex2Shell:
→ Four Plex Media Server flaws: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656
→ Chained, they hand over the owner's admin token and code execution
→ Attacks seen installing an XMRig cryptominer and a Linux proxy backdoor
→ Details went public 16 Oct; exploitation reported from 17 Oct
→ The fix has existed since August: version 1.43.3.10861

What to do: update Plex Media Server to 1.43.3.10861 or later, don't expose it to the internet unless you need to, and check for processes you don't recognise.
